{.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} census %>% filter(age < 25, sex == 'Female') ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 80 × 8 census_year state_fips_code `arrange()` sorts the rows by a certain variable (or set of variables) ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} census %>% arrange(age) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A 65000 1 Female White 5 2000 Michigan 57400 1 Female White 6 2000 Pennsylvania 27150 1 Male White 7 2000 Florida 50090 2 Male White 8 2000 Florida 6000 2 Male White 9 2000 New York 68020 2 Female Chinese 10 2000 New York 17000 2 Male Two major races # ℹ 490 more rows # ℹ 2 more variables: marital_status , total_personal_income ``` ::: ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## `arrange()` Can do **descending order** too with the `desc()` function! ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} census %>% arrange(desc(age)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 500 × 8 census_year state_fips_code total_family_income age sex race_general 1 2000 Louisiana 8100 93 Female White 2 2000 Illinois NA 87 Female White 3 2000 West Virginia 0 87 Male White 4 2000 Delaware 46200 85 Female White 5 2000 Indiana 8000 85 Male Black 6 2000 New York 15570 83 Male White 7 2000 New York 8800 82 Female White 8 2000 Massachusetts 34300 82 Female White 9 2000 New York 55000 81 Male White 10 2000 Minnesota 0 81 Female White # ℹ 490 more rows # ℹ 2 more variables: marital_status , total_personal_income ``` ::: ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## `arrange()` Can arrange by **multiple variables** too: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} census %>% arrange(age, sex) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 500 × 8 census_year state_fips_code total_family_income age sex race_general 1 2000 Texas 9200 0 Male Black 2 2000 New York 65000 1 Female White 3 2000 Michigan 57400 1 Female White 4 2000 Florida 48000 1 Male White 5 2000 New York 13000 1 Male White 6 2000 Pennsylvania 27150 1 Male White 7 2000 New York 68020 2 Female Chinese 8 2000 Maryland 95500 2 Female White 9 2000 Oregon 9300 2 Female White 10 2000 Michigan 20340 2 Female White # ℹ 490 more rows # ℹ 2 more variables: marital_status , total_personal_income ``` ::: ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## `summarize()` `summarize()` computes summary statistics and collapses data into row(s) that show those summary statistics ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} census %>% summarize(mean_income = mean(total_family_income, na.rm = TRUE), sd_income = sd(total_family_income, na.rm = TRUE), size = n()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 1 × 3 mean_income sd_income size 1 57411. 70732. 500 ``` ::: ::: - Can compute multiple measures ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## `group_by()` + `summarize()` Add `group_by()` to `summarize()` to calculate summary statistics *by specified grouping variable(s)* ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} census %>% group_by(state_fips_code) %>% summarize(mean_income = mean(total_family_income, na.rm = TRUE), sd_income = sd(total_family_income, na.rm = TRUE), size = n()) %>% filter(size > 10) %>% arrange(mean_income) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 14 × 4 state_fips_code mean_income sd_income size 1 Washington 20079. 12980. 11 2 Louisiana 34899. 42097. 12 3 Ohio 40748. 26796. 23 4 Indiana 46738. 32291. 17 5 Florida 46848. 31787. 39 6 Pennsylvania 51685 44823. 26 7 Illinois 55972. 42426. 21 8 New York 57064. 44793. 43 9 Texas 58240. 72468. 37 10 Michigan 59160 27403. 14 11 Massachusetts 59506. 38984. 12 12 Georgia 60488. 52199. 18 13 California 73142. 69338. 62 14 New Jersey 77498 80288. 15 ``` ::: ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Tip: `count()` `count()` is a short-cut for `group_by()` + `summarize(n())` ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} census %>% group_by(sex) %>% summarize(n()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 2 × 2 sex `n()` 1 Female 232 2 Male 268 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} census %>% count(sex) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 2 × 2 sex n 1 Female 232 2 Male 268 ``` ::: ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## `group_by()` + `mutate()` Adding `group_by()` allows functions (e.g., `sum()`) to operate on variables *by specified grouping variable(s)* Let's start with this summary dataset: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} temp <- census %>% count(marital_status, sex) temp ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 12 × 3 marital_status sex n 1 Divorced Female 21 2 Divorced Male 17 3 Married/spouse absent Female 5 4 Married/spouse absent Male 9 5 Married/spouse present Female 92 6 Married/spouse present Male 100 7 Never married/single Female 93 8 Never married/single Male 129 9 Separated Female 1 10 Separated Male 2 11 Widowed Female 20 12 Widowed Male 11 ``` ::: ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## `group_by()` + `mutate()` ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} temp %>% mutate(p = n / sum(n)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 12 × 4 marital_status sex n p 1 Divorced Female 21 0.042 2 Divorced Male 17 0.034 3 Married/spouse absent Female 5 0.01 4 Married/spouse absent Male 9 0.018 5 Married/spouse present Female 92 0.184 6 Married/spouse present Male 100 0.2 7 Never married/single Female 93 0.186 8 Never married/single Male 129 0.258 9 Separated Female 1 0.002 10 Separated Male 2 0.004 11 Widowed Female 20 0.04 12 Widowed Male 11 0.022 ``` ::: ::: **Q:** What is the denominator for the proportions in the new `p` variable? ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## `group_by()` + `mutate()` ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} temp %>% group_by(marital_status) %>% # added this! mutate(p = n / sum(n)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 12 × 4 # Groups: marital_status [6] marital_status sex n p 1 Divorced Female 21 0.553 2 Divorced Male 17 0.447 3 Married/spouse absent Female 5 0.357 4 Married/spouse absent Male 9 0.643 5 Married/spouse present Female 92 0.479 6 Married/spouse present Male 100 0.521 7 Never married/single Female 93 0.419 8 Never married/single Male 129 0.581 9 Separated Female 1 0.333 10 Separated Male 2 0.667 11 Widowed Female 20 0.645 12 Widowed Male 11 0.355 ``` ::: ::: **Q:** *Now* what is the denominator for the proportions in the new `p` variable? # Now: type of data objects ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Stat 241 `R` Data Objects So Far: **Data frames**: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} crash_data <- read_csv("data/pdx_crash_2018_page1.csv") class(crash_data) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "spec_tbl_df" "tbl_df" "tbl" "data.frame" ``` ::: ::: ::: {.fragment} **(Atomic) Vectors**: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} pretty_colors <- c("steelblue", "seagreen", "goldenrod") class(pretty_colors) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "character" ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.fragment} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} size <- 3 class(size) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "numeric" ``` ::: ::: ::: - The last two are both examples of what are called **atomic vectors**. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## R Objects: Vectors * **Vectors** are the fundamental building blocks of data in `R`. + Each column in a data frame is an atomic vector! + Come in **2** flavors! ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} * **Flavor 1:** **Atomic vectors** + Homogeneous collections of the same type. + Confusingly, people usually just call these *vectors*. ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} * **Flavor 2:** **Generic vectors** + Heterogeneous collections of any type of `R` objects. + Commonly called *lists*. ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Deep Dive into (atomic) vectors * Let's explore the common types and how to interact with them. * This will allow us to use vectors to **do useful things**, * Understand logical statements and `dplyr` more robustly, and * **debug our code** more effectively! ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ### Flavors of Atomic Vectors :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width='50%' .fragment} **Logical**: TRUEs and FALSEs ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} happy <- c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE) class(happy) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "logical" ``` ::: ::: **Numeric**: Integers, real numbers (double-precision floating point numbers) ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} x <- c(1, 4, 5) class(x) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "numeric" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} x <- c(1L, 4L, 5L) class(x) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "integer" ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width='50%' .fragment} **Character**: Strings (contains 1 or more characters) ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} animals <- c("mountain goat", "lemur", "capybara") class(animals) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "character" ``` ::: ::: **Factors**: Strings with order ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} animals <- as.factor(animals) class(animals) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "factor" ``` ::: ::: ::: :::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ### Factors versus Characters :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width='50%'} **Character**: Strings (contains 1 or more characters) ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} animals <- c("mountain goat", "lemur", "capybara") class(animals) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "character" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} typeof(animals) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "character" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} str(animals) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` chr [1:3] "mountain goat" "lemur" "capybara" ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width='50%' .fragment} **Factors**: Strings with order ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} animals <- as.factor(animals) class(animals) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "factor" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} typeof(animals) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "integer" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} str(animals) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Factor w/ 3 levels "capybara","lemur",..: 3 2 1 ``` ::: ::: What?! ::: :::: - If you want to read more about this rabbit hole, [go here](https://developer.r-project.org/Blog/public/2020/02/16/stringsasfactors/index.html). ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ### Concatenation Atomic vectors are created and combined with `c()`. :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width='50%'} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} x <- 5 x ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 5 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} y <- c(4, 1, 7) y ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 4 1 7 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width='50%' .fragment} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} z <- c(y, x, c(20)) z ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 4 1 7 5 20 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} quick <- c(2:5, 13) quick ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 2 3 4 5 13 ``` ::: ::: ::: :::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ### Checking Type :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width='50%'} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} is.logical(c(FALSE, TRUE)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} is.logical(c(0, 1)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] FALSE ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width='50%' .fragment} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} is.factor(c("mountain goat", "lemur", "capybara")) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] FALSE ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} is.character(c("mountain goat", "lemur", "capybara")) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE ``` ::: ::: ::: :::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ### Checking Type :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width='50%'} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} is.integer(1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] FALSE ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} is.double(1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} is.numeric(1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} is.atomic(1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width='50%' .fragment} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} is.integer(1L) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} is.double(1L) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] FALSE ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} is.numeric(1L) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} is.atomic(1L) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE ``` ::: ::: ::: :::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ### Type Coercion * R will often change the type of a vector with no warning. * Usually it makes the smart choice. :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width='50%' .fragment} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} y <- c(4, 1, 7) class(y) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "numeric" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} z <- c(y, "cat") class(z) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "character" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} z ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "4" "1" "7" "cat" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} z <- c(y, 3L) class(z) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "numeric" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} z ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 4 1 7 3 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width='50%' .fragment} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} a <- c(FALSE, 4) class(a) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "numeric" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} a ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0 4 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} b <- c(NA, 4) class(b) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "numeric" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} b ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] NA 4 ``` ::: ::: ::: :::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ### Operator Coercion * Functions and operators (like `+`, `-`, `*`, etc.) will often try to convert a vector to an appropriate type. * Once we are writing our own functions, we will consider building in tests to ensure the user provided the correct type. :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width='50%' .fragment} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} 1L + 3.1415 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 4.1415 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} log(TRUE) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} sum(c(FALSE, TRUE, TRUE)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 2 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width='50%' .fragment} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} TRUE & FALSE ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] FALSE ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} TRUE | FALSE ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} TRUE & 7 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} FALSE | !7 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] FALSE ``` ::: ::: ::: :::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ### Changing Type * We can also explicitly change the type, for example: :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width='50%' .fragment} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} as.logical(c(0, 6.4, 1)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] FALSE TRUE TRUE ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} as.character(c(FALSE, TRUE, TRUE)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "FALSE" "TRUE" "TRUE" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} as.integer(pi) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 3 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width='50%' .fragment} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} as.numeric(c(FALSE, TRUE, TRUE)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0 1 1 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} as.double(c("01", "02", "03")) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 1 2 3 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} as.double(c("one", "two", "three")) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] NA NA NA ``` ::: ::: ::: :::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Vectorized * R is built to work with vectors. * Many operations are **vectorized**: will happen component-wise when given a vector as input. :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width='50%' .fragment} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} y <- c(4, 1, 7) y + 4 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 8 5 11 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} y * 2 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 8 2 14 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width='50%' .fragment} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} x <- c(-4, 0, 2) y + x ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 0 1 9 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} rnorm(n = 3, mean = c(-5, 0, 5)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] -4.4109965 0.4945386 4.5288123 ``` ::: ::: ::: :::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Vectorized: Caution :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width='50%' .nonincremental} * We need to be careful with vectorization! ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} my_pets <- data.frame( name = c("Dude", "Pickle", "Kyle", "Nubs"), type = c("dog", "cat", "cat", "cat"), age = c(8, 6, 4, NA), birthplace = c("Washington", NA, "Utah", NA) ) my_pets ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` name type age birthplace 1 Dude dog 8 Washington 2 Pickle cat 6 3 Kyle cat 4 Utah 4 Nubs cat NA ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width='50%'} Want the rows where `name` is either Dude or Kyle. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} library(tidyverse) my_pets %>% filter(name == c("Dude", "Kyle")) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` name type age birthplace 1 Dude dog 8 Washington ``` ::: ::: * What happened? ::: :::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Recycling * R recycles vectors if they are not the necessary length. + Notice we got NO error but that wasn't what we wanted. ::: {.fragment} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} library(tidyverse) my_pets %>% filter(name %in% c("Dude", "Kyle")) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` name type age birthplace 1 Dude dog 8 Washington 2 Kyle cat 4 Utah ``` ::: ::: ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Indexing a Vector :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width='50%'} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} x <- c(4, 6, 9) x[1] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 4 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} x[-1] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 6 9 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width='50%' .fragment} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} x[c(2, 4)] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 6 NA ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} a <- c(2, 4) x[a] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 6 NA ``` ::: ::: ::: :::: # So what about **generic vectors/lists**? ::: {.fragment} Recall they are heterogeneous collections of any type of `R` objects. ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ### Lists Think of these as the **most general** way to store things. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} groceries <- list() groceries$new_seasons <- c("apples", "goat cheese", "pizza slice") groceries$safeway <- c("black beans", "tortillas") groceries$peoples_food_coop <- c("squash", "tea", "fresh greens") groceries$budget <- data.frame(stores = c("new_seasons", "safeway", "peoples_food_coop"), fund = c(100, 25, 200)) class(groceries) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "list" ``` ::: ::: .cell-output-stdout} ``` $new_seasons [1] "apples" "goat cheese" "pizza slice" $safeway [1] "black beans" "tortillas" $peoples_food_coop [1] "squash" "tea" "fresh greens" $budget stores fund 1 <- c("Valentine's", "President's") feb <- list(groceries = groceries, holidays = holidays) feb ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` $groceries $groceries$new_seasons [1] "apples" "goat cheese" "pizza slice" $groceries$safeway [1] "black beans" "tortillas" $groceries$peoples_food_coop [1] "squash" "tea" "fresh greens" $groceries$budget stores fund 1 new_seasons 100 2 safeway 25 3 peoples_food_coop 200 $holidays [1] "Valentine's" "President's" ``` ::: ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ### Indexing lists Distinguishing between `[ ]` and `[[]]` ::: {.fragment} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} thing1 <- feb$groceries[3] thing1 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` $peoples_food_coop [1] "squash" "tea" "fresh greens" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} class(thing1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "list" ``` ::: ::: :::
::: {.fragment} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} thing2 <- feb$groceries[[3]] thing2 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "squash" "tea" "fresh greens" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} class(thing2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "character" ``` ::: ::: ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## [`[ ]` versus `[[ ]]`](https://r4ds.had.co.nz/vectors.html#lists-of-condiments) `x[[1]][[1]]` is what? ::: {.fragment} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](img/innerobject2.png){fig-align='center' width=30%} ::: ::: ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Data Frames Let's relate `list()`s to our favorite R object: `data.frame()`s! * `data.frame()`s are `list()`s. * Each variable of a `data.frame()` is an atomic `vector()`. * The `vector()`s all have the same length but not necessary the same class. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Data Frames ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} my_pets ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` name type age birthplace 1 Dude dog 8 Washington 2 Pickle cat 6 3 Kyle cat 4 Utah 4 Nubs cat NA ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} my_pets$name ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "Dude" "Pickle" "Kyle" "Nubs" ``` ::: ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Data Frames ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} str(my_pets[1]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 'data.frame': 4 obs. of 1 variable: $ name: chr "Dude" "Pickle" "Kyle" "Nubs" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} str(my_pets[[1]]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` chr [1:4] "Dude" "Pickle" "Kyle" "Nubs" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} my_pets[1, 2] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "dog" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} my_pets[1, ] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` name type age birthplace 1 Dude dog 8 Washington ``` ::: ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Thoughts about R data objects * We can create and interact with (atomic) **vectors** and **lists** (generic vectors). * When writing and debugging code, it is a good idea to check the `class()` of an object. * R will sometimes change the type of an object without telling us (but based on our actions). * **Vectorization** makes `R` code speedy but also can cause you to do something you didn't mean to do. * While we will primarily interact with `vector()`s and `data.frame()`s, we will sometimes need `list()`s. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ### Next time ::: {.nonincremental} - Joining, reshaping, and tidying data! ::: ### Next Week ::: {.nonincremental} - Spatial data in `R` :::

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
